Coastal Cities Race to Adapt as Sea Levels Rise Faster Than Predicted

Engineers, economists and residents are confronting an uncomfortable question: how much of the shoreline can realistically be defended?

By Margaret Ellison and Tomás Reyes · Updated 6 hours ago · 9 min read

When the storm surge arrived in late October, it did not behave the way the models had anticipated. The water climbed over seawalls that had been reinforced only two years earlier, flooded subway entrances and lingered in low-lying neighborhoods for days. Officials later acknowledged that the barriers were designed for a climate that no longer exists.

Across dozens of coastal cities, planners are now abandoning the assumption that the past is a reliable guide to the future. Satellite measurements show that global sea levels have been rising at an accelerating pace, and several recent studies suggest the most pessimistic projections may have been conservative rather than alarmist.

A costly dilemma

The financial stakes are enormous. Protecting a single mile of densely populated waterfront can cost hundreds of millions of dollars, and the maintenance burden persists for decades. Smaller municipalities, which often depend on property taxes from the very homes most at risk, face a particularly vicious cycle: as insurers retreat and valuations decline, the revenue needed to fund adaptation shrinks.

"We are essentially being asked to choose which communities deserve protection," said Dr. Alicia Moreno, a hydrologist who advises several regional authorities. "That is not a technical decision. It is a profoundly political and ethical one, and we have been reluctant to admit it."

The ocean does not negotiate. Our infrastructure was built on the premise of a stable coastline, and that premise has quietly evaporated.

Some cities have embraced so-called managed retreat, gradually relocating residents away from the most vulnerable areas and allowing wetlands to reclaim the land. The approach is controversial. Critics argue that it disproportionately affects lower-income households, while proponents insist that delaying the inevitable merely increases the eventual cost.

Engineering meets ecology

A growing number of engineers are advocating hybrid solutions that combine conventional concrete structures with restored natural buffers. Oyster reefs, mangrove forests and salt marshes can absorb wave energy, trap sediment and adapt dynamically as conditions change. Unlike static walls, these living shorelines can, in principle, grow alongside rising water.

Yet the evidence remains incomplete. Natural defenses take years to mature, and their performance during extreme events is harder to quantify. Insurance companies and federal agencies, which typically demand rigorous cost-benefit analyses, have been hesitant to finance projects whose effectiveness cannot be precisely predicted.

  • Elevated roadways and pumping stations are being prioritized in the most exposed districts.
  • Building codes are being revised to require higher foundations for new construction.
  • Several utilities are relocating critical substations inland.

Modeling teams increasingly publish their code so that others can scrutinize the assumptions. A typical configuration snippet looks like this:

scenario = load_projection("ssp5-8.5", horizon=2100)
surge = simulate(scenario, barrier_height=4.2)

The human dimension

For residents, the debate is anything but abstract. Lucia Fernandes, whose family has lived on the same street for three generations, described the anxiety of watching the tide creep higher each season. "Every time it rains heavily, we move the furniture upstairs," she said. "My children think it is normal. That terrifies me."

Community organizers say that trust is the scarcest resource of all. Previous relocation programs were plagued by bureaucratic delays and unfulfilled promises, leaving many people deeply skeptical of official reassurances. Rebuilding that trust, they argue, will require transparency about the risks and a genuine willingness to share decision-making power.

Economists warn that the consequences will ripple far beyond the shoreline. Ports handle a substantial proportion of international trade, and disruptions to shipping could reverberate through global supply chains. Meanwhile, the gradual depreciation of coastal real estate threatens the balance sheets of banks and pension funds that hold mortgages in those regions.

Still, there are reasons for cautious optimism. Cities that began planning early have demonstrated that thoughtful, incremental investments can substantially reduce damage. Rotterdam, often cited as an exemplary case, has integrated water storage into public squares, parking garages and parks, turning a vulnerability into a distinctive feature of urban design. Read more about Rotterdam's approach.

The window for deliberate action is narrowing, however. As one planner put it, the choice is no longer between adapting and doing nothing, but between adapting thoughtfully now or chaotically later.
